Hi Product Hunt community, I’m Bharath, founder of Inferock.

Every team running LLMs in production pays for calls that came back empty, truncated, timed out, or returned broken JSON. You usually find out from a user, and you can’t prove it to anyone.

Inferock sits between your app and the provider and measures every call against a published baseline for quality, speed and cost. Each call gets a receipt that Inferock produces itself, so it doesn’t depend on the provider’s word.


Two ways to use it:

- Inferock Watch: bring your own OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini keys. Free. You get the receipts and a monthly loss report. Enroll in the credit program and objectively broken calls accrue credits you can spend on Serve.

- Inferock Serve: serverless, pay-per-token inference through us. This is where your credits get spent.

How credits work: credits are non-cash, expire after 12 months, and are capped at $1,000 in the wallet and $1,000 applied per month. They cover verified, billed, unrecovered objective failures: downtime and timeouts, empty or truncated output, invalid structured output, billing and cache anomalies.

name: Tiden
tagline: Intent verification for coding agents
description: Tiden verifies your coding agents built what you actually asked for. Most checks run inside the session that wrote the code, so the tests agree with it by construction. Tiden keeps your intent as requirements that branch and merge like code, and checks every change against that record. The verdict comes from tests run in your environment; no model grades the diff. You decide what merges, and production errors trace back to the release. Works beside Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Copilot.

nodes.body:
Hi Product Hunt, I'm Nikita, and this is Tiden, the product we've been building for the past year. It's for engineering teams shipping agent-written code every day who want to let agents do the coding while keeping control of what ships.

Qase is a software testing platform used by tens of thousands of builders, and 9 years of building it for them taught us a lot about how quality work gets done. Last year that changed on our own team: agents started producing most of the code, and the rest of our process didn't speed up with it. Review, testing, release, keeping requirements current: all of it became bottlenecks.

Other engineering teams tell the same story. A gaming publisher I talked to, with about 1k+ developers, saw pull request volume go up 4 to 5 times while the number of features they shipped stayed flat. A payments company described 10 times the coding output and 10% more delivery.

The problem underneath it

An agent session produces the code, the tests that pass on that code, and the docs describing what it built. The next session reads those docs as fact. Every artifact agrees with every other one, because they all came from the same place. A QA automation lead at a tax and accounting platform put it best: "If you have an agent that decides what to build, and then another agent is grading what's being built against what was actually built, you're essentially encoding the wrong thing. Your tests will pass, they'll be green, but it wasn’t what you wanted."

The two usual fixes, another rules file in the repo and better AI code review, both sit inside that same loop. The judge has to sit outside it.

What Tiden does

Tiden is that judge. It's intent verification for coding agents: it sits beside your agents, whichever ones you use, and verifies that what they built is what you actually asked for. It keeps that intent as specs, versioned like code, and checks every change against them rather than against the session that produced it.

Every agent session becomes a closed loop:

  • A session hook captures what you asked for before the first edit

  • The change comes back as a requirement for you to review; requirements branch and merge like code

  • Tiden picks the tests the change touches, runs them in your environment, and the agent fixes what fails before anything merges

  • The gate is tied to the spec. Red tells the agent what to fix. Green is a pass you can defend, with the evidence attached

  • In production, an error traces back to the release, the change and the prompt behind it, and the fix comes with the test that was missing

Tiden works beside Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Copilot, and belongs to none of them. Specs live as one versioned record every agent reads from, instead of a growing pile of markdown. You set the thresholds and the gates, and a person approves anything the loop can't settle.

One limit, stated plainly: Tiden checks the work against what you asked for. Whether you asked for the right thing is still a human judgment.

Get started

Tiden is live at https://tiden.ai. The CLI installs in one command, the docs are at https://docs.tiden.ai, and Starter and Team both come with a 14-day free trial. If you'd rather talk to us first, there's a short form on the site: https://tiden.ai/contact.

What I'd like from you

Honest feedback over upvotes. Where does your team feel this gap most: review, regression, release, or production? What would make you trust an external check?

I do believe that no model grading is the right call. Our evals had deterministic routing tests before it could ship. That split is what kept people trusting it. How so you handle cases where deterministic tests aren't enough, like "this should feel fast"

Hi Product Hunt Community,

I am Nitin, and I am product manager for Tiden. Today, after six months of building, we are finally sharing it with you.

Here is the problem in one line: your agents are fast, but your delivery is not.

Coding agents can write a change in minutes. Yet that same change often takes days to reach production. The PR waits because nobody is sure what else it touches. CI catches a regression on the second push. A reviewer spots a function the agent invented. The code got faster. The delivery did not.

The data backs this up. In Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey, trust in AI accuracy fell to 29%, and 66% of developers said they spend more time fixing "almost right" code. Faros AI found that teams with high AI adoption merge 98% more PRs, while review time rises 91%. Google's DORA research put it simply: AI amplifies what is already there.

The market's answer so far has been a point AI tool for every phase: one for context, one for tests, one for PR review, one for release signals. They are faster cars on old roads. The lifecycle underneath was designed for humans who read specs and follow instructions. Agents sometimes do, sometimes do not, and sometimes invent things that were never there. Throwing more AI at the problems AI creates is not a solution. It is an illusion.

So we started from a blank slate. Tiden is a continuous verification system for agentic coding teams, built around one idea: an enforceable boundary.

Here is how it works:

1. Before a single line of code: Tiden builds a context graph of your system, linking features, requirements, tests and components. When a change comes in, the agent walks that map, finds what is affected and fills the gaps. The result is captured as intent, and that intent becomes the boundary the code must deliver against.

2. Clear context, not all the context: the coding agent gets exactly what is relevant, so it ships in fewer iterations and gets it right more often.

3. Before the PR, not after it: Tiden picks the functional and regression tests that matter for this change, based on requirements and risk, and runs them before a PR exists. Only when that quality gate passes can the agent open the PR.

4. After the merge: release evidence is assembled automatically, and production issues are tracked, feeding the next change.

In our own use, cycle time from starting a change to releasing it came down by almost half. Not because code was written faster, but because the most of rework loops simply stopped happening.

Tiden is built by the team behind Qase, so almost a decade of quality assurance thinking has gone into how verification should work when agents write the code.

We would love your honest feedback:

- Where does your agentic workflow break down today?

- What would you need to trust an agent's change without reading every line?

- What is missing?

You can start a 14-day trial at tiden.ai. I will be here all day answering questions.

Google Cloud Run is one of the best places to run an app: it scales to zero, bills only while your code works, and runs on Google's own network. Getting in is the hard part. It has its own rules, and many common architectures break on them quietly: a cron inside the process fires late or twice, a worker waiting on a queue stalls, uploads on local disk vanish, sessions in memory sign people out. So most teams stay on a PaaS and keep paying for hours their app sleeps, because the path there isn't clear.

We moved our own apps this year and wrote down every step. Exodus turns that into a path your coding agent follows, to upgrade any app to Cloud Run:

→ Is your app ready? One line to your agent installs our open-source CLI and checks the repository on your machine: processes, data, settings and every pattern that breaks or bills while idle.
→ What will it cost? Today's bill against Cloud Run at Google's list prices, with your traffic, 16 regions and a 12-month forecast.
→ How should it be built? Your app drawn on Google Cloud, rebuilt by our 50+ playbooks: each change with the reason, the replacement and the order.
→ Then move. Your agent works the plan, a commit per task, and the report ticks itself. exodus check in CI keeps it that way.
→ Starting from zero? Describe the idea and Exodus designs it for Cloud Run block by block: services, database, stack, and the bill at launch and in a year.

Your code never leaves your machine, we run no AI of our own, and we never sign in to your Google Cloud. For the Cloud Run team: Exodus runs on Cloud Run itself, one Rust service with Firestore, scaling 0 to 3.

nodes.body:
hey developers 👋

the problem

Coding agents write good code, but they’re still tied to your laptop. Close the lid and they die, your RAM caps how many you can run, and you still have to check every diff yourself.

the solution

Reason splits the agent in two. The brain (the harness) runs detached in the cloud and drives separate hands (a sandboxed machine). Sessions survive crashes, deploys and lost boxes, can be rewound, and hop between cloud Linux, a cloud Mac and your own Mac without losing state.

And it does more for less. On GPT-6 Astra, Reason scores 65.1 vs Codex’s 62.5 on the Coding Agent Index at 22% lower cost per solved task, and it’s 15–23% cheaper per attempt on every benchmark. On GPT-6.1 Sol, median cost per task is 34% below Codex. Every score links to a public Harbor job.

What’s inside

Built for the cache: a small set of tools and a short prompt, and each request only appends, so every turn is fully cache-eligible. That’s where the savings come from.

A computer per session: full desktop, live browser and terminals, with your saved logins. Take the wheel any time.

PRs with proof: walkthrough video and before/after screenshots go on every PR, then review, CI fixes and the merge queue.

Bring your own subs: plug in the coding plans you already pay for. When one hits its rate limit, Reason rolls over to the next.

Resume any agent: import a Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Devin session and keep going.

nodes.body:
Maia 300 is Microsoft’s next-generation AI inference platform, announced October 12, 2026. Microsoft also said it will expand Azure Maia to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027.

Problem: Running AI at scale is limited by power and cost, and Microsoft has to serve a lot of models to a lot of products like Copilot and Teams. Microsoft’s answer is to design its own silicon alongside the GPUs it buys.

Solution: Maia 300 is built inference-first. Per Microsoft, it targets long-context reasoning, low-latency conversation and multi-step agent work. Microsoft says it will become the primary AI inference system for its own products and services. Satya Nadella is quoted calling it “our biggest bet yet on our own silicon.”

What Microsoft reports about the design:

  • Eight HBM4 memory stacks with 18.0 TB/s peak bandwidth, and a 950 W power rating

  • Compute chiplets on TSMC’s N2P process, with a multi-chiplet design that separates compute, memory control and I/O

  • Support for low-precision formats such as MXFP4 to cut memory and bandwidth needs

  • A custom AI transport for scale-up communication across accelerators and racks

  • One rack holds 96 accelerators in a 167 kW power envelope, with 27.6 TB of HBM

Performance: these are Microsoft’s own claims, with no independent benchmarks. It says Maia 300 delivers 40% more tokens per megawatt. Coverage disagrees on what that is compared against, with some outlets saying the previous Maia and others saying leading GPU-based systems, so I’d check Microsoft’s post. It also expects a Maia 300 rack to reach up to 7x the token throughput of Maia 200 at rack scale.

Timeline:

  • Maia 200 is already running production workloads in the US, Europe and Australia

  • Maia 300 begins production deployments in 2027

Hey Product Hunt 👋 I'm Dylan, and I built Specreel.

AI has made building software dramatically faster, and my own projects were no exception. When I did find time to record a demo video, it was out of date within a week. Since I'm always spinning up something new, it kept happening. So I set out to solve my own problem.

The one thing that never went stale was my end-to-end tests. They recorded the exact same browser flows on every build, and when the app changed, they failed instead of quietly drifting.

So Specreel treats them as one artifact: a recorded browser flow. Replay it = demo. Share it = send. Assert it = test.

Three ways in:
• Paste your app's URL → we open it in a real browser, suggest the flows worth showing, and turn them into a narrated, shareable demo gallery. Behind a login? Add a test account and we sign in first.
• Already on Playwright? Turn on tracing and point the open-source CLI at your trace.zip files (JS/TS, Python, Java, .NET). A GitHub Action republishes on every green build, so your demo is never older than your last passing build.
• Prefer to just ask? The MCP server lets Claude Code or Cursor run the whole loop.

Things I cared about:
– Captions come straight from your actions and assertions. They're deterministic and need no AI. AI narration and voiceover are opt-in, bring your own key.
– Typed passwords and one-time codes are masked automatically.
– You never change your tests. The demo is just an output.
– Cloud is free to start. Team ($39/mo) adds scheduled re-checks and Slack/email alerts when a flow breaks. Viewers and reviewers are always free.

description: Hold ⌘ in any Mac app to see every keyboard shortcut, read live from its menus. Click a row to run it. Free, no time limit. Keysi Pro ($14.99 once) teaches the ones you keep missing: a quiet reminder, spaced-repetition drills, and "New" marks after updates.

nodes.body:
Hey PH! 👋

Keysi started because I used to love CheatSheet, the little app that shows a Mac app's keyboard shortcuts when you hold a key, and it died on macOS Sonoma with nothing quite replacing it. Turned out the API it needed never actually broke, so I rebuilt the idea from scratch (no shared code).

What it does:
- Hold ⌘ and see every shortcut of the app you're in, read live from its menus. Every row is clickable: it's the actual menu, so clicking "Export…" runs Export.
- It tells you when macOS itself will intercept a shortcut before you ever press it, instead of leaving you wondering why nothing happened.
- Ten built-in cheat sheets for shortcuts no menu lists (Figma, Slack, Notion, Obsidian, Excel, Word, Ghostty, Vim, tmux and Emacs), plus an editor for your own. Keysi looks inside your terminal, so the Vim and tmux sheets fire for Vim and tmux, not just the terminal app.
- It reads the shortcuts you rebound yourself in Xcode, VS Code and JetBrains IDEs.
- Localized into 9 languages.

The part people don't expect, in Keysi Pro: it notices when you pick something from a menu with the mouse that already has a shortcut, and quietly tells you once. Practice Mode then drills the ones you keep missing with spaced repetition. After an app updates, the overlay marks the shortcuts the update added, and if you keep clicking a command that has no shortcut at all, Keysi suggests a free key combination and where to set it.

One honest limitation: you can't type to search while holding ⌘ (a technical constraint, not a missing feature; happy to explain in the comments). A separate hotkey, ⇧⌘K, opens a proper searchable panel.

Pricing: the app is free, with no time limit and no account: the overlay, click-to-run, search, custom sheets and Markdown/PDF export. Keysi Pro is $14.99 once: Shortcut Coach, Practice Mode, and integrations like Raycast, Alfred and Shortcuts. You get 14 days of Pro when you grant access, and when they end the app keeps working as the free tier. macOS 14 or later.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt 👋

I wanted a tool that would help me **think through system design faster during interviews**. Most diagramming tools make you spend too much time dragging boxes, connecting arrows, and arranging everything before you can focus on the actual problem.

So I built **Diagramly**, a whiteboard where you can type your ideas, let AI turn them into diagrams, and get straight to solving the problem.

For example, type:

`Client -> API -(HTTPS)-> Orders, Payments -> Orders DB`

Press Enter, and you get a clean, hand-drawn diagram with the layout handled for you. You can keep editing it with text, drag-and-drop, drawing tools, or AI.

Here's what makes Diagramly different:**

- ⚡ Go from idea to diagram in seconds:** Describe a system in plain English or use a simple typing syntax. AI turns your ideas into diagrams you can refine, rather than making you build everything from scratch.
- 🤖 AI that works with your canvas:** Ask it to create a system, add a component, restructure a flow, or change an existing diagram. Every AI change can be reverted.
- 🎯 Views built for presenting:** Create multiple views on the same canvas, each highlighting a different part of your system. Switch between them with keyboard shortcuts during a presentation, keeping the audience focused on what matters.
- 🎬 Turn diagrams into presentations:** Press `Shift + P` to turn your frames into slides that reveal information step by step.
- 🎨 Six visual styles:** Switch between paper, notebook, blueprint, chalkboard, whiteboard marker, and ink & neon with one click.
- 📝 Cheat sheets and visual notes:** Combine diagrams with bullets, steps, flows, tables, and takeaways. Publish them as shareable cheat sheets.
- 🌐 Embed and share anywhere:** Share view-only links or embed diagrams in docs, wikis, websites, and social media posts.

name: AURORA Lifeline
tagline: Know who a cyclone will cut off, before the roads close
description: Turns the official IMD cyclone bulletin into a district plan: which PHCs, hospitals and villages will lose road access, how likely, when, and what to move first. Gemini reads the bulletin, 1,000+ WeatherNext and ECMWF storm futures run over every road, and code inserts every number. Officers approve everything. Open source, misses published.

nodes.body:
Hi Product Hunt 👋

Every cyclone season in India, warnings get better and evacuations save lives. But after landfall the roads flood, bridges and culverts close, and villages lose their only road to a hospital. A woman in labour, a snakebite, a dialysis patient: for days, help can't get through.

Three days out, a district control room knows where the storm is going. What it doesn't know is which health centre will be cut off, how likely that is, when, and what to move there before the roads close. Today that's worked out by phone calls and experience.

AURORA Lifeline starts from the official IMD bulletin and answers those four questions:
• Gemini reads the bulletin PDF and quotes every value; code checks each one against the PDF.
• Over a thousand storm futures from Google DeepMind WeatherNext and ECMWF, aligned to IMD's track, put wind, rain and surge on 5.4 lakh road segments, hour by hour.
• For each future, a fast network search finds when every village and health facility loses its last road to a public hospital. You get a chance and a time window, never a falsely precise hour.
• It ranks where to stage earthmovers, each with a deadline and its reason.
• Gemini drafts the advisory in Telugu, Hindi or English, but it never writes a number: code inserts every figure. It's read aloud with Gemini TTS and exported as a CAP alert, and an officer approves before anything goes out.
• An agent built with Google's Agent Development Kit answers officers' questions from the run's facts, with citations.

Try the replay of Cyclone Montha (Andhra Pradesh, Oct 2025) exactly as it looked 62 hours before landfall, then Cyclone Dana in Odisha. Geography is configuration, so a new state is a config file and a map extract.

How it evolved: we started with "which roads flood?" and ended with "which PHC loses its last road, and when?". That shift made us build our own road network instead of using routing APIs. It also made us strict about uncertainty: a chance and a window, labelled priors, and validation against Sentinel-1 radar with our misses published on the Proof page.

It's open source (Apache-2.0) and was selected in the top 10 of Track 05 at Build with AI: Code for Communities. We'd love feedback, especially from anyone in disaster management or public health. What would make this useful in your district?
Love that AURORA Lifeline turns the cyclone bulletins into a clear cutoff forecast, so responders can see who gets isolated before the roads close.

Almost every developer has been there: you're integrating an external service (Stripe, GitHub, Shopify, Clerk, etc.), and you're waiting for a webhook.
You open a tunnel, send a test event, and get a wall of raw JSON. Now you have to manually inspect headers, check payload shapes, and spend 20 minutes writing TypeScript interfaces (or worse, typing it as `any`).

What is Payload Peek?
Payload Peek turns real incoming HTTP requests into typed code in seconds. No account, no CLI installation, no setup hassle:

1. Instant Inbox: Get a private webhook URL immediately upon visiting.
2. Inspect: Watch real HTTP requests arrive in real time with headers, methods, and formatted payloads.

Cloud Run's serverless autoscaling means the webhook receiver scales up instantly to handle bursty webhook traffic and scales down to zero when idle, with zero infrastructure management.

name: LegacyFixer
tagline: Python dependency security scans with optional fix PRs
description: Compared with Dependabot and Renovate, LegacyFixer focuses on security-first scanning of Python dependencies. It reports vulnerability findings even when an automated fix is not appropriate, and creates a fix pull request only when its policy and validation checks allow it. Each scan produces an explicit outcome, including detect-only (NO_ACTION) when no fix PR is created. LegacyFixer runs as a GitHub App on Google Cloud Run.

nodes.body:
Hi Product Hunt!

LegacyFixer began without a business plan or even a product idea. I was curious about AI and wanted to explore one question: Could someone without formal programming education build a real software product by working side by side with AI?

From February to August 2026, I worked with ChatGPT to find out. We discussed architecture, made technical decisions, wrote and revised code, investigated failures, and tested repeatedly. I didn't hand the project to an autonomous AI agent. Codex helped mainly with code reviews and testing.

It wasn't easy. We first ran the application on a separate server, then migrated it to Google Cloud Run and moved PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL. There were mistakes, unexpected problems, and a great deal to learn.

What surprised me was how much I loved the process. Some nights I worked until midnight, completely absorbed in what we were building. The experiment had become something personally meaningful.

Today, LegacyFixer is a working GitHub App that scans Python dependencies for security vulnerabilities and creates controlled fix pull requests only when its validation checks allow. Otherwise, it reports findings without changing the repository.

I'm here for technical feedback, critical evaluation, and real-world use cases. 

LegacyFixer exists because a human and AI worked side by side.

Thanks for taking a look!
